lines.text: Your database is running.
Your servers are online.
But users are seeing stale data.
Requests are slowing down.
And one small change takes days to ship.
Is your system actually working well?
To answer that, we'll follow Chapter 1 of Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications, first edition.
lines.say: To answer that, we'll follow Chapter one of Martin Klepman's Designing Data Intensive Applications, first edition.

lines.text: The chapter rests on three words, each really a question.
First: does your system keep working when components go wrong? That's reliability.
Second: can it handle growth? That's scalability.
Third: can people understand, operate, and change it over time? That's maintainability.
Each symptom points to one of them.
What makes an application data-intensive? Data, not CPU power, is its main challenge.
lines.say: What makes an application data intensive? Data, not C P U power, is its main challenge.

lines.text: Its volume, its complexity, or how fast it changes.
The building blocks are familiar. Databases store data for later.
Caches remember expensive results.
Search indexes find records by keyword.
Streams pass messages asynchronously.
Batch jobs crunch large piles of data.
Real applications combine them: a client calls your code.
It writes to a primary database: the official copy.
A cache keeps common reads fast.
A search index makes the same data searchable.
Background workers take changes from a queue and update both.
Now watch a write update the database.
Until a worker catches up, the cache still holds the old value. The next read returns stale data: our first symptom.
No product promised these copies would agree; by wiring them together, you made that promise.
You're not just using data systems anymore. You're designing one.
That broken promise brings us to question one: reliability.
A reliable system does what users expect, tolerates their mistakes, stays fast enough, and blocks abuse, even when things go wrong.
A fault is when one part of the system misbehaves.
A failure is when the whole system stops giving users the service they expect.
Requests reach two database replicas, copies of the same data.
One replica crashes. That's a fault.
Traffic shifts to the other replica; users never notice. That's fault tolerance.
Now the same app with only one replica.
Same fault: the replica crashes.
Requests have nowhere to go; users see errors. The fault became a failure.
You can't prevent every fault. Pick the kinds you'll tolerate, and design so they don't become failures.
Where do faults come from? First, hardware. Picture 10,000 disks.
lines.say: Where do faults come from? First, hardware. Picture ten thousand disks.

lines.text: Assume a 30-year mean time to failure per disk: a statistical figure, not a lifespan.
lines.say: Assume a thirty-year mean time to failure per disk: a statistical figure, not a lifespan.

lines.text: 10,000 disks, divided by 30 years times 365 days, is about one failure per day.
lines.say: Ten thousand disks, divided by thirty years times three hundred sixty-five days, is about one failure per day.

lines.text: It's a simplified illustration: independent failures, constant rate. But at this scale, failure is routine.
The classic defense is redundancy: RAID arrays, dual power supplies, spare machines.
lines.say: The classic defense is redundancy: raid arrays, dual power supplies, spare machines.

lines.text: Today, software can also tolerate losing a whole machine.
That enables rolling upgrades, one node at a time, without downtime.
Second, software. These five nodes all run the same code.
On June 30, 2012, a leap second triggered a Linux kernel bug.
lines.say: On June thirtieth, twenty twelve, a leap second triggered a Linux kernel bug.

lines.text: Many applications hung at the same moment.
Redundancy assumes faults are independent, like those disks. Software faults often aren't.
A spare doesn't help if it runs the same bug.
Runaway processes, slow dependencies, and cascading failures can hit many nodes at once.
The third source is people. Say someone edits one timeout, typing milliseconds where they meant seconds.
The change rolls out everywhere, and services start failing one after another.
One study of large internet services found operator configuration errors were the leading cause of outages.
Fault tolerance has a weak spot: error-handling code rarely runs, so bugs hide there.
So some teams inject faults on purpose, like Netflix's Chaos Monkey.
It randomly terminates servers, so recovery code runs regularly.
The system notices and replaces the node automatically.
Killing a cache worker on purpose tests whether you'd spot stale data before users do.
For human mistakes, add safety nets: tests, sandboxes, and gradual rollouts, so a bad timeout hits only a few servers.
Plus fast rollback, monitoring, and safe tools to recompute data.
Question two: scalability. Requests often slow down because load has grown.
Saying 'our system is scalable' sounds like a yes-or-no answer. It isn't.
Ask instead: if load grows in a particular way, what are our options?
First, describe today's load with a few numbers, called load parameters.
Requests per second, reads versus writes, users online at once, cache hit rate, or skew: a few extreme cases.
A historical example: Twitter, around 2012.
lines.say: A historical example: Twitter, around twenty twelve.

lines.text: Posting a tweet averaged about 4,600 requests per second.
lines.say: Posting a tweet averaged about forty-six hundred requests per second.

lines.text: Home timeline reads, your feed, ran around 300,000 per second.
lines.say: Home timeline reads, your feed, ran around three hundred thousand per second.

lines.text: The hard part was fan-out: one request multiplying into many lookups or writes.
First came fan-out on read: opening your timeline meant looking up everyone you follow and merging their tweets.
That's heavy work on every read, and Twitter struggled to keep up.
So Twitter switched to fan-out on write: each user gets a cached timeline, like a mailbox.
A new tweet is copied into every follower's mailbox.
Reading becomes a cheap lookup.
That trade paid off because reads dominate: roughly 65 timeline reads for every tweet posted.
lines.say: That trade paid off because reads dominate: roughly sixty-five timeline reads for every tweet posted.

lines.text: But writes aren't free: 4,600 tweets a second, times an average of 75 followers each.
lines.say: But writes aren't free: forty-six hundred tweets a second, times an average of seventy-five followers each.

lines.text: That's about 345,000 timeline insertions every second.
lines.say: That's about three hundred forty-five thousand timeline insertions every second.

lines.text: Now add a celebrity. Some accounts had over 30 million followers.
lines.say: Now add a celebrity. Some accounts had over thirty million followers.

lines.text: One tweet from them meant 30 million insertions, yet Twitter aimed to deliver tweets to followers within about five seconds.
lines.say: One tweet from them meant thirty million insertions, yet Twitter aimed to deliver tweets to followers within about five seconds.

lines.text: Next to the average of 75, that bar runs off the chart.
lines.say: Next to the average of seventy-five, that bar runs off the chart.

lines.text: Most accounts have modest followings; a tiny few have enormous ones. That's skew.
The load parameter that matters here isn't just the average. It's the distribution of followers.
Twitter then moved toward a hybrid. Most users' tweets still fan out on write, into precomputed timelines.
Tweets from the few accounts with huge followings skip that step and are fetched when you read.
When you open your timeline, the two are merged by time.
The lesson: a few outliers can decide the whole design. That's true for speed, too.
What does 'slow' actually mean? Follow one request: network, a queue, the work itself, network back.
Response time is all of it: what the client waits for.
Latency is narrower: the time spent waiting to be handled.
Repeat the same request, and the times still vary.
Random delays creep in: a garbage-collection pause, a context switch, a lost packet, a page fault, even a vibrating server rack.
So response time is a distribution. This histogram groups 1,000 simulated requests by duration.
lines.say: So response time is a distribution. This histogram groups one thousand simulated requests by duration.

lines.text: A percentile is the response time that a given share of requests stays under.
The median, or p50, is the middle: half are faster. That's 111 milliseconds.
lines.say: The median, or p fifty, is the middle: half are faster. That's one hundred eleven milliseconds.

lines.text: At p95, 95 out of 100 are faster.
lines.say: At p ninety-five, ninety-five out of one hundred are faster.

lines.text: At p99, 99 out of 100 are faster: 234 milliseconds.
lines.say: At p ninety-nine, ninety-nine out of one hundred are faster: two hundred thirty-four milliseconds.

lines.text: These high percentiles describe the tail: the slowest requests.
Now add a few long pauses: 20 requests, just 2%, take 0.8 to 2 seconds.
lines.say: Now add a few long pauses: twenty requests, just two percent, take zero point eight to two seconds.

lines.text: The median barely moves, 111 to 112, and the mean rises only a little.
lines.say: The median barely moves, one hundred eleven to one hundred twelve, and the mean rises only a little.

lines.text: But p99 jumps from 234 to 1,473 milliseconds.
lines.say: But p ninety-nine jumps from two hundred thirty-four to fourteen hundred seventy-three milliseconds.

lines.text: Averages hide this. High percentiles reveal it.
Why care about the tail? Amazon, for example, has historically described internal service targets in terms of p99.9.
lines.say: Why care about the tail? Amazon, for example, has historically described internal service targets in terms of p ninety-nine point nine.

lines.text: Slow requests often come from customers with the most data, frequently the most valuable ones.
Percentile targets often go into service level agreements. For example: median under 200 milliseconds, p99 under 1 second.
lines.say: Percentile targets often go into service level agreements. For example: median under two hundred milliseconds, p ninety-nine under one second.

lines.text: Why not go higher? At p99.99, Amazon judged the cost outweighed the benefit.
lines.say: Why not go higher? At p ninety-nine point nine nine, Amazon judged the cost outweighed the benefit.

lines.text: Tails get worse with fan-out. Say one user request makes 100 backend calls.
lines.say: Tails get worse with fan-out. Say one user request makes one hundred backend calls.

lines.text: Each call, independently, has a 1% chance of being slow.
lines.say: Each call, independently, has a one percent chance of being slow.

lines.text: The request can't finish until every call returns, so one slow call makes it slow.
The chance that at least one call is slow is 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰.
lines.say: The chance that at least one call is slow is one minus zero point nine nine to the power of one hundred.

lines.text: That's about 63%: a 1% problem now slows down most user requests.
lines.say: That's about sixty-three percent: a one percent problem now slows down most user requests.

lines.text: This assumes calls are independent and the request waits for all of them. It's called tail latency amplification.
Where you measure matters. A server works on only a few requests at once.
One slow request at the front makes the fast ones wait: head-of-line blocking.
The server logs them as fast, but the client waited. Measure on the client side.
Load tests should keep sending without waiting for replies, or queues look unrealistically short.
One last trap: combining measurements. In this illustration, three servers each report a p99.
lines.say: One last trap: combining measurements. In this illustration, three servers each report a p ninety-nine.

lines.text: Averaging them gives 571 milliseconds, but averaging percentiles is meaningless.
lines.say: Averaging them gives five hundred seventy-one milliseconds, but averaging percentiles is meaningless.

lines.text: Instead, merge the histograms first, then read the p99 from the result: 208 milliseconds.
lines.say: Instead, merge the histograms first, then read the p ninety-nine from the result: two hundred eight milliseconds.

lines.text: Tools like HdrHistogram and t-digest make merging cheap, across servers and time windows alike.
lines.say: Tools like H D R Histogram and tee digest make merging cheap, across servers and time windows alike.

lines.text: Back to growth. Scaling up means moving to one bigger machine.
Scaling out spreads work across many smaller machines that share nothing. Real systems often mix both.
Stateless services keep no data between requests, so adding copies behind a load balancer is fairly easy.
A stateful database is harder: its data must be split and copied across machines.
Workloads differ too: 100,000 one-kilobyte requests per second, versus 3 two-gigabyte requests per minute.
lines.say: Workloads differ too: one hundred thousand, one-kilobyte requests per second, versus three, two-gigabyte requests per minute.

lines.text: Both move about 100 megabytes per second, but need very different designs.
lines.say: Both move about one hundred megabytes per second, but need very different designs.

lines.text: There's no universal recipe.
A long-standing rule of thumb was to keep the database on one node until cost or availability forced distribution.
Going distributed isn't the automatic next step.
Question three: maintainability, and our last symptom, a small change that takes days to ship.
Most of the cost of software comes after launch: fixing bugs, keeping it running, adapting it, adding features.
Three ideas help. First, operability: make life easy for the people who keep the system running.
Say a node needs a patch: move its traffic away, update it, and bring it back. No machine is special.
That takes visibility into what's happening, good automation, sensible defaults you can override, and predictable behavior.
Second, simplicity: make the system easy to understand.
Without it, you get a big ball of mud: tangles and special cases everywhere.
Much of that is accidental complexity: it comes from how we built the system, not from the problem it solves.
Good abstractions remove it. With SQL, you just say which data you want.
lines.say: Good abstractions remove it. With S Q L, you just say which data you want.

lines.text: Storage on disk, concurrent clients, and crash recovery stay hidden underneath.
In our example, that might mean moving scattered cache-invalidation code into one module.
lines.say: In our example, that might mean moving scattered cache invalidation code into one module.

lines.text: Third, evolvability: make future change easy.
Requirements keep moving: new use cases, shifting business priorities, new regulations, growth.
Remember Twitter switching from fan-out on read to fan-out on write? That was an architecture-level change.
An evolvable system lets you make changes like that in small, safe, backward-compatible steps.
Back to our three symptoms.
Stale data is reliability: your team promised the cache and index would match the database, and that promise broke.
Slowing requests are scalability and performance: growing load, and a tail hidden by averages.
And days to ship a small change is maintainability: accidental complexity makes the system hard to operate and change.
Running and online was never the same as working well.
So take three questions back to your team. Which faults can we tolerate without users noticing?
Which load parameter would force us to rethink our architecture?
And what makes our system unnecessarily difficult to operate or change?
Answer those honestly, and you'll know what 'working well' means for you.
